doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

chapter: Big band years and the lean years
title: Quitting Harry James over bop; lean years digging ditches
summary: Conniff tells James he doesn't feel bop and quits, gets no calls for two years, works as a ditch laborer in Reseda, and decides to write for the paying public with strong rhythm.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And bop was kind of supposed to be a floating type of rhythm on top cymbals and stuff. You weren’t supposed to hear it, you were supposed to feel it here. You were supposed to feel what he was trying — and I don’t know, I never felt that, so I said, “Hey you know, Harry, I just don’t feel that kind of music,” and you know, “maybe it’s time you got another boy.” And his jaw dropped. He looked at me and he couldn’t believe what I was saying. And he said, “well, okay.” So I left the band. For two years I thought all I had to do was pick up the phone and call my old pals, you know, like Sonny Burke at Decca and Paul Weston was at Columbia Records. And I called all of them and told them, “hey I’m free now, I’m not writing steady all the time for Harry, I’m available.” And boy, for two years the phone hardly rang. And finally after sitting waiting for the phone to ring for two years I got so discouraged I thought — I had a wife and a mother I was supporting, and three children, and we were living out in Reseda, and I thought, I’ve got to go get a job. I can’t go on like this. I took a job — they were converting a ten acre, it was a melon field, into a subdivision out in Reseda. And I went out and took a job as a laborer, cleaning up the ditches behind the ditch digger. Where he’d make mistakes on the corner, I’d clean the ditches. And I got to thinking, wow, what happened? Which way did they go, you know. I was making, in 1940, Artie was paying me $300 a week, you know, which in those days was a lot of money. And here I am out digging ditches, you know, for $60 a week. But it gave me a lot of time to think. But anyway I took an awful long — I’ve got to start pinning my answers down, it took a long time to answer your question — but I started thinking completely different about writing arrangements. I thought, what if I started writing for the people that paid the bills, the people that listened, the people that bought the records you know. And I started thinking more along the lines of commercially, and I thought about, you know everything in life is rhythm. Our heartbeat is a rhythm, each day is a rhythm, the sun rises and sets to a rhythm, and the ocean tides go in and out to a rhythm, the cycles of the seasons are a rhythm. And I thought rhythm is very important in our life, and I made the rhythm very predominant. And then I remembered when I first started thinking about the opposite sex. There was a little girl down the street that I had a terrible crush on. I must have been I don’t know, ten, eleven, twelve, something like that. And she was always singing a song, it was [sings], “ooooh, would you like to take a walk — ooooh, do you think it’s going to rain — and something’s gonna come from that” is the name of the song. And to this day, I’ve heard that song once in a while, people will play an old record or a disc jockey. It still moves something. I thought, if I can catch the songs that people fell in love to the first few times, I’ve got a wonderful idea. And that’s what I did.
